subtype: Distressed and disappointed by exams and comparison [Expressing]
passage:
Day one. Results were out at noon. Farida read her marks on the school portal, closed the laptop and said nothing at lunch. Her mother, Nandini, noticed she left her rice untouched.
Day four. Farida snapped at her younger brother over a borrowed pen, then muttered, "Don't bother with me, I'm useless. Everyone got more." Nandini stopped her chopping. She didn't lecture about studying harder or list other children's scores. She simply sat down by Farida and said, "That sounds heavy. Tell me more."
Day nine. Farida was still quiet and still saying she'd never be good at anything. Nandini called the school counsellor that morning and booked a time, and sat beside Farida while they spoke.

qa.q: What did Farida leave untouched at lunch on day one?
qa.a: She left her rice untouched.

qa.q: What might Farida be feeling when she says 'I'm useless'?
qa.a: She is probably deeply disappointed and hopeless, comparing herself with others; snapping at her brother may show the hurt spilling over.

qa.q: Why did Nandini contact the school counsellor on day nine?
qa.a: Because Farida stayed quiet and kept saying she'd never be good at anything, so the hopeless feeling wasn't fading and needed caring, professional attention.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt seeing Farida still quiet on day nine?
qa.a: Nandini was probably worried that Farida's hopeless talk was lasting, which is why she called the school counsellor and sat beside her.

grounding: A teen after poor results goes silent, snaps and calls herself useless; the family responds with caring attention, not lectures.

subtype: Distressed and disappointed by exams and comparison [Expressing]
passage: "I was your age when I failed my second-year exams, Avni," said Jomon, turning the pages of an old photo album on the verandah. "I told everyone I was useless and stopped speaking at meals. My friends' results were all better, and I couldn't stand the comparison." He tapped a photograph of a stern man. "Your great-grandfather wanted to shout, I could see it. Instead he sat next to me on this bench every evening and said nothing for a week. Then he asked what I was afraid of. I told him." Jomon closed the album. "If you ever feel that heavy, come to me. Don't sit alone with it."

qa.q: Where did Jomon's father sit with him every evening?
qa.a: He sat next to Jomon on the bench on the verandah every evening.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling after failing his exams?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and ashamed, shown by calling himself useless, stopping speaking at meals and being unable to bear the comparison with friends.

qa.q: What could Avni do if she ever feels that heavy?
qa.a: She could go to Jomon or another trusted adult and say what she's afraid of, instead of sitting alone with it.

qa.q: How might Jomon's father have felt as he sat silently?
qa.a: He probably wanted to shout or fix things, but he chose to stay close and wait, showing worry and care.

grounding: A teen after poor exam results says they are useless; caring attention from family, not lectures, helps.

subtype: Distressed and disappointed by exams and comparison [Expressing]
passage:
Results came out the same day Jaya's whole family arrived for her cousin's wedding. The flat in Lucknow was packed, the power kept cutting, and the aunties were comparing marks before lunch.
Her cousin Dhruv had topped his school. Jaya had scraped through maths.
She went silent. When Bade Papa said, "See Dhruv, beta, learn from him," she snapped, "Great, thanks, very helpful," and walked out.
In the stairwell, her mother found her sitting on the steps. Jaya muttered, "I'm useless. Everyone thinks so."
Her mother sat beside her, sari and all, in the dusty stairwell. She didn't lecture. "I don't think so. I'm sorry that happened in front of everyone. How are you feeling, really?"
"Stupid. Like nothing I do counts."
"You count to me. Marks are one day."
She stayed with Jaya until she stopped shaking, then walked back in and quietly asked the relatives to stop comparing.

qa.q: What had Dhruv done in his results?
qa.a: Dhruv had topped his school.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she said "I'm useless"?
qa.a: Jaya felt humiliated and hopeless about her marks, made worse by being compared to Dhruv in front of the family.

qa.q: What did Jaya's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She sat with Jaya without lecturing, apologised for the public comparison, asked how she felt, and asked the relatives to stop comparing.

qa.q: How might Bade Papa have seen his comment?
qa.a: He probably thought he was encouraging Jaya, not realising how crushing the comparison felt on a bad day.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager going silent, snapping and calling herself useless after poor results, and a parent responding with care rather than lectures.

subtype: Distressed and disappointed by exams and comparison [Expressing]
passage:
For three days after the Class 10 results, Lokesh barely left his room in their Bengaluru flat. He skipped cricket. When his father, Vikas, asked about lunch, he said, "What's the point of anything?" He said it again at dinner. And again the next day.
Vikas put aside his speech about retests and tuition.
That night he knocked and sat on the edge of the bed. "You've said 'what's the point' a lot. I'm worried about you. Not the marks. You."
Lokesh's face crumpled. "I feel like I've let everyone down. Like nothing's going to get better."
Vikas stayed close. He asked, gently, whether those thoughts ever felt dangerous. Lokesh said he didn't know.
Vikas said, "Thank you for telling me. We'll get help, together," and that same night he called a helpline with Lokesh beside him. Next morning they saw the school counsellor together.

qa.q: For how many days did Lokesh barely leave his room?
qa.a: For three days after the Class 10 results.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling after the results?
qa.a: Lokesh felt hopeless and ashamed, as if he had let everyone down and nothing would get better.

qa.q: Which of Vikas's choices were most important?
qa.a: Putting aside talk of marks, naming his worry, asking gently about dangerous thoughts, and getting help that same night and the next morning.

qa.q: How might Vikas have felt hearing "What's the point of anything" again and again?
qa.a: He probably felt deeply worried and frightened for his son, which is why he acted urgently instead of lecturing.

grounding: The scene shows persistent hopelessness after exams and a parent giving urgent, caring attention instead of lectures.

subtype: Distressed and disappointed by exams and comparison [Expressing]
passage:
"Farhan, how did you do?"
"Don't."
Sharmila sat down on the steps beside him anyway. "Okay. I won't ask."
Farhan stared at the result sheet. "Fifty-two in science. My dad's going to say I'm wasting his money. And he's right. I'm useless."
"You're not useless."
"You got ninety. You don't get it."
Sharmila took a breath. She wanted to say, it's just one exam, you'll do better. She didn't.
"You're right, I don't know exactly how it feels. But I can see it hurts a lot."
Farhan's shoulders dropped. "I'm scared to go home."
"Want me to stay while you call your mum first? She might help with your dad."
He nodded. His mother picked up on the second ring. Sharmila heard her voice through the phone, soft: "Come home, beta. We'll talk together. You're not in trouble with me."

qa.q: What mark did Farhan get in science?
qa.a: Fifty-two in science.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling about going home?
qa.a: Farhan felt scared and ashamed, worried his father would say he was wasting money, and called himself useless.

qa.q: What did Sharmila get right as a friend?
qa.a: She didn't lecture or minimise, acknowledged that it hurt, and helped him call his mother so a caring adult could step in.

qa.q: How did Farhan's mother respond, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She said softly that he wasn't in trouble with her and they'd talk together, showing that the family's reaction could be caring, which eased his fear.

grounding: The dialogue shows a teenager snapping and calling himself useless after poor results, fearing family reaction, and being met with care.

subtype: Distressed and disappointed by exams and comparison [Expressing]
passage: The day the Class 10 results came out, I went silent for about six hours. Seventy-one percent. Charu, my little sister, had got 94 in her Class 8 exams the same week, and Baba had already told the whole building. At dinner someone said, "Next time, more focus," and I pushed the plate away and said, "What's the point. I'm useless. There's no point in me." Charu stopped chewing. I remember Baba starting to answer with a lecture, and Maa putting her hand on his arm. She came to my room straight after, sat on the floor by my bed and said, "Anirban, I heard what you said, and I'm not leaving you alone with it tonight." She stayed until one. Before I slept, she called the helpline number the school gives out, with me beside her, and the next afternoon we saw the counsellor together. Charu slid a note under my door: "you're not useless, you taught me fractions." I still have it.

qa.q: What percentage did Anirban get?
qa.a: Anirban got seventy-one percent.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when pushing the plate away?
qa.a: Anirban felt crushed and hopeless, set beside Charu's 94 and stung by 'Next time, more focus'; saying 'no point in me' showed despair, not just disappointment.

qa.q: What did Maa do that mattered most?
qa.a: Maa stopped the lecture, stayed with Anirban that night instead of leaving it, called the helpline together before sleep and went with Anirban to the counsellor the next afternoon.

qa.q: What was it like for Charu to hear 'I'm useless'?
qa.a: Charu was startled, stopping mid-chew, and later tried to help by sliding a note saying Anirban had taught her fractions.

grounding: It shows a teenager going silent and calling themself useless after poor results, and a parent giving urgent, caring attention instead of a lecture.
